connection: ScratchPad contains prior experiments and the student knows local methods. No TimeClock requirement currently needs ref, out, or in parameters. Add an isolated ScratchPad parameter-passing experiment without distorting a production repository API.
objectives: Explain why out lets a method report a lookup result and success/failure without a nullable return type or a thrown exception.
Write TryGetOpenEntry(int employeeId, out ClockEntry? entry), a new method modeled on GetClockEntry's real nullable-return shape but demonstrating the out alternative.
Explain why ref would let a method reassign a caller's ClockEntry? variable entirely, not just mutate the object it currently refers to.
Explain why in is not needed anywhere in this codebase, since no method here takes a large struct by value.

visuals.title: out reports a second value on the way out
visuals.explanation: bool TryGetOpenEntry(int employeeId, out ClockEntry? entry) returns whether the lookup succeeded AND assigns entry -- two pieces of information from one call.

visuals.title: The caller must handle both outcomes
visuals.explanation: if (repository.TryGetOpenEntry(1, out var entry)) uses entry only inside the branch where TryGetOpenEntry returned true -- the compiler enforces entry is definitely assigned by that point.

visuals.title: ref lets a method replace what the caller's variable refers to
visuals.explanation: A ref ClockEntry? parameter could reassign the caller's variable to a completely different object, not just mutate the current one.

visuals.title: in protects a large struct from being copied
visuals.explanation: None of this codebase's parameters are large structs, so in has no real use here -- it exists for a category of problem this domain does not have.

preQuiz.prompt: What does TryGetOpenEntry(1, out var entry) let you avoid, compared to the real async GetClockEntry(1)?
options: Nothing conceptually different -- it is a synchronous alternative to the same nullable-result idea, useful for comparing the two patterns side by side
It avoids ever needing a null check
It makes the lookup run faster
preQuiz.explanation: Both patterns communicate 'found or not found' -- out ClockEntry? plus a bool return is one C# idiom for it; a nullable return type (the real GetClockEntry's choice) is another.

preQuiz.prompt: Inside if (repository.TryGetOpenEntry(1, out var entry)) { ... }, what does the compiler guarantee about entry?
options: entry is definitely assigned to a non-null ClockEntry inside the if block, because out parameters must be assigned before the method returns
entry might still be null even though TryGetOpenEntry returned true
entry is only valid outside the if block
preQuiz.explanation: C# requires every out parameter to be assigned before the method returns -- combined with a true return value, this is the whole point of the Try-pattern.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does this course's real domain have no genuine use for the in modifier?
options: in exists to avoid copying large structs by value; every struct-like value this codebase passes around (int, DateTime) is small enough that copying is already cheap and idiomatic
in is deprecated in modern C#
in only works with reference types
preQuiz.explanation: in is a performance tool for large structs -- this codebase's value types (int, DateTime) are exactly the small, cheap-to-copy kind in was never meant to optimize.

concept.title: Ordinary parameters receive values
paragraphs: By default, a method receives a copy of the argument value. Reassigning the parameter does not replace the caller's variable.
For a class variable, the copied value is a reference, so both sides can still observe mutation of the same object.

concept.title: out returns an additional value
paragraphs: A Try-style method can return success as bool and place the found value in an out parameter.
This is useful when absence is expected, but it should not be added to a production API unless callers genuinely need that shape.
concept.code:
static bool TryRead(string text, out int value) =>
    int.TryParse(text, out value);

concept.title: ref and in communicate special intent
paragraphs: ref permits the method to replace caller-visible storage. in passes by reference while preventing reassignment through that parameter.
Both are specialized tools. ScratchPad lets you observe them without distorting TimeClock contracts.
concept.code: static void Increment(ref int value) => value++;

commit: session-08: teach parameter passing with ref, out, and in
review: The lab uses scratchpad because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.
Earlier production code, tests, and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does TryGetOpenEntry return bool instead of just returning ClockEntry??
options: Both are valid designs for the same problem -- the Try-pattern with out is one C# idiom, a nullable return (the real GetClockEntry's choice) is another; this session teaches the out alternative specifically
ClockEntry? cannot be returned from a synchronous method
bool is required by the out keyword
postQuiz.explanation: There is no technical requirement to use bool+out over a nullable return -- it is an idiom choice, and this session's point is recognizing both idioms.

postQuiz.prompt: What would go wrong if TryGetOpenEntry's implementation had a code path that returned true without assigning entry?
options: The code would not compile -- C# requires every out parameter to be definitely assigned before the method returns, on every path
entry would default to a valid open ClockEntry automatically
Nothing -- out parameters are optional to assign
postQuiz.explanation: Definite assignment of out parameters is enforced by the compiler, not just a convention -- this is exactly why callers can trust entry after a true return.

postQuiz.prompt: Could ref have been used instead of out for TryGetOpenEntry's entry parameter?
options: Technically yes, but it would require the caller to initialize entry before the call, for no benefit -- out is the correct, idiomatic choice when the method fully determines the value
No, ref and out are interchangeable in every situation with no difference
No, ref only works with value types
postQuiz.explanation: ref requires the variable to already have a value going in; out does not -- since TryGetOpenEntry's caller has no meaningful value to provide beforehand, out is the right tool.

reflections: Now that you have both GetClockEntry (nullable return) and TryGetOpenEntry (out parameter) side by side, which would you choose for a new method, and why?
Can you think of a genuine (not contrived) use for ref anywhere in this codebase as it might grow?
Why does 'this domain doesn't need in' feel like a legitimate lesson outcome rather than an incomplete one?
whatBreaks: Adding a code path in TryGetOpenEntry that returns true without assigning entry would fail to compile -- the definite-assignment rule catches this at compile time rather than allowing a null-reference bug at runtime. Confusing ref with out would lead you to expect a caller-provided initial value for entry that TryGetOpenEntry does not need or use.
summary: out lets a method return a second value (here, whether an open entry was found) alongside its normal return type, with the compiler enforcing definite assignment. ref would let a method reassign a caller's variable to an entirely different object -- a capability this codebase's real, ordinary-reference mutation patterns (Session 8) never need. in exists to avoid copying large structs, and this domain's small value types (int, DateTime) never pay that cost in the first place.
